options: Requires you to choose an EC2 instance type
Invokes your code in response to events
Requires you to configure high availability manually
Built-in monitoring and logging with Amazon CloudWatch

questions.question: What are the two core components of Lambda?
questions.explanation: Slide 13 notes: an event source publishes events to Lambda, and the function is your custom code that processes them.

questions.question: Because Lambda is a fully managed service, high availability and fault tolerance are built in without additional configuration.
questions.explanation: Slide 14: Lambda provides built-in availability and fault tolerance with no configuration on your part.

questions.question: With Lambda, you configure the CPU, network and I/O throughput for each function separately from memory.
questions.explanation: Slide 14: you configure memory, and AWS handles the details such as CPU, network and I/O throughput.

questions.question: A company loads a social media stream into Amazon Kinesis in real time and wants to compute hashtag trends and store them in DynamoDB. Which Lambda use case is this?

questions.question: Match each Lambda use case with an example.
questions.explanation: Slide 15 lists web apps, real-time stream processing, backends, data processing, chatbots, Alexa skills and IT automation as Lambda use cases.

pairs.right: API Gateway endpoint invokes Lambda to read data from DynamoDB
Conversational interface built with Amazon Lex
Start and stop EC2 instances on a fixed schedule
S3 or DynamoDB invokes Lambda when data changes

questions.question: When you create a Lambda function, which of the following do you define? Select more than one answer.
questions.explanation: Slide 16: you define permissions, initiating events, the runtime and deployment package, and configuration such as memory, timeout and concurrency.
options: Settings such as memory, timeout and concurrency
A runtime and a deployment package
The EC2 instance type that runs it

questions.question: To use a language that Lambda does not support natively, you can implement a custom runtime.

Total concurrent invocations across all functions in an account per Region (soft quota)
Prevents concurrency from rising too quickly during a spike; cannot be modified
Keeps environments warm to avoid cold starts

questions.explanation: Slide 38: per function, you can set a concurrency limit to prevent overwhelming a downstream system.

A failure caused by low memory
Startup latency when Lambda must initialize a new environment to run the function

questions.question: Drag each workload to the better ECS launch type.
questions.explanation: Fargate: variable, low overhead, small tests, scheduled batch. EC2: predictable, price-optimized, compliance, excess capacity.

items.item: Use reserved instances to reduce cost

questions.question: You have batch workloads that run on a schedule and want low operational overhead. Which ECS launch type?
questions.explanation: Fargate suits scheduled batch workloads and low overhead.

questions.question: You already have excess EC2 capacity. Which ECS launch type makes sense?
questions.explanation: Excess EC2 capacity → EC2 launch type.

questions.question: What is Amazon EKS?
questions.explanation: EKS runs Kubernetes; conformant, compatible, secure by default.
options: A managed service to run Kubernetes on AWS

questions.question: A team needs a private, managed place on AWS to store their Docker images for Amazon ECS. Which service?
questions.explanation: ECR is the fully managed container registry.

questions.question: A company already uses Kubernetes on premises and wants a managed Kubernetes service on AWS. Which should they choose?
questions.explanation: EKS runs conformant Kubernetes.

questions.question: Order the evolution of deployment models.
questions.explanation: Bare metal → VMs → containers, each improving utilization and portability.
items: Bare-metal servers
Virtual machines
Containers

questions.question: Order the steps to push an image to Amazon ECR.
questions.explanation: Create repo → build → tag → login → push.
items: Create the ECR repository
Build the image
Tag the image with the repository URI
Authenticate Docker to the registry
Push the image

questions.question: A Dockerfile contains these instructions, in this order: start from the Ubuntu 22.04 image, install Nginx, copy the website files, create a log directory. Drag each line to the image layer it creates (Layer 1 is the bottom). Lines that are not part of this Dockerfile, or are only comments, go to "Not a layer".
questions.explanation: Each Dockerfile instruction creates a read-only layer, built from the bottom (base image) up, in the order written. Comments do not create layers.

items.item: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y nginx
RUN yum -y update && yum -y install httpd

questions.question: Using the course example, put the image layers in order from bottom to top.
questions.explanation: The base layer is at the bottom; each later Dockerfile instruction adds a read-only layer on top.
items: Base image
Software update and Apache installation
Expose port 80
Copy the shell script
Run the shell script

questions.question: Which of the following are orchestration tools for Docker containers? Select more than one answer.
questions.explanation: Orchestration options include native Docker Swarm, open-source Kubernetes, and Amazon ECS. EC2 is compute and a Dockerfile only builds an image.

questions.question: What are the advantages of containers over virtual machines?
questions.explanation: Containers share the host OS kernel, so they are lightweight, efficient and fast, start faster than VMs, and allow shared or isolated libraries.
options: More operating systems to patch, which improves security
Each container runs its own full guest operating system
Slower to start but better hardware utilization
Lightweight, efficient and fast, with libraries that can be shared or isolated

questions.question: Containers are well matched to support microservices.
questions.explanation: Each microservice can run in its own isolated container and be updated, deployed and scaled independently.

questions.question: The container runtime shares the host operating system's kernel.
questions.explanation: That is why containers are lighter than VMs, which each carry a full guest OS.

questions.question: If you change one instruction in a Dockerfile and rebuild, every layer of the image is always rebuilt.
questions.explanation: Only the layers that changed are rebuilt, which keeps images small and builds fast.

questions.question: The shipping container analogy shows how standardization increased agility. In this sense, what does abstraction mean?
questions.explanation: Slide 7 notes: abstraction is a way of hiding the working details of a subsystem; it separates concerns to facilitate interoperability and platform independence.
options: Packing every item by hand into whatever vessel is available
Hiding the working details of a subsystem so people are removed from those details
Giving each shipment its own custom container size
Tracking the weight of each item before it is loaded

questions.question: Before standardized shipping containers, transporting goods was slow, inefficient and costly because goods came in no standard weight, shape or size.
questions.explanation: Slide 7: uniformly sized containers later simplified loading, unloading, storing and transferring, improving efficiency and reducing costs.

questions.question: According to the course, which of the following can a container package? Select more than one answer.
questions.explanation: Slide 8: a container contains everything the application needs to run, such as application code, runtime engine, system tools, system libraries and settings. It shares the host OS kernel instead of carrying a full guest OS.
options: A separate full guest operating system

questions.question: Containers provide operating system virtualization so that an application and its dependencies run in resource-isolated processes.
questions.explanation: Slide 8 notes: containers provide OS virtualization so you can run an application and its dependencies in resource-isolated processes.

questions.question: A single server can host only one container at a time because each container needs its own OS kernel.
questions.explanation: Slide 8 notes: a single server can host several containers that all share the underlying host system's OS kernel.

questions.question: On a bare-metal server, one application needs an updated version of a shared library that is incompatible with the other applications on the host. Why is this a problem?
questions.explanation: Slide 9: on bare-metal servers, library versions must be shared across applications, so an incompatible update for one application causes problems for the others.
options: Library versions must be shared and kept in sync across all applications on the server
Each application already has its own isolated copy of the library

questions.question: With bare-metal servers, hardware costs are the same whether the server runs at 0 percent or 100 percent utilization.
questions.explanation: Slide 9 lists inflexible hardware costs: you pay the same regardless of utilization.

questions.question: A host runs three VMs. Compared with running the same applications in containers, what is a drawback of this setup?
questions.explanation: Slide 10 notes: the virtualization layer is heavy; three VMs means three operating systems, more patching and space, and redundant copies of the same OS and libraries.
options: Resource utilization is worse than on bare metal
The VMs must share one set of library versions
The applications cannot be isolated from each other
Three operating systems to patch and update, possibly with the same OS and libraries installed three times

questions.question: Containers start up and shut down more slowly than VMs, but they use less disk space.
questions.explanation: Slide 11 notes: containers can be started up and shut down faster than VMs, which means better utilization of the underlying hardware.

questions.question: A developer's containerized application runs in development and must behave the same in staging and production. Which container characteristic makes this possible?
questions.explanation: Slide 11: containers are highly portable; because they isolate software from other layers, code runs identically from development and staging through production.
options: Containers are rebuilt from source in every environment
Containers are highly portable and their code runs identically across environments
Containers each include their own full guest OS
Containers require identical physical hardware in each environment

questions.question: Which of the following describe Docker as a container virtualization platform? Select more than one answer.
questions.explanation: Slide 14: Docker is a lightweight container virtualization platform with tooling to create, store, manage and run containers, and it integrates easily with automated build, test and deployment pipelines.
options: It integrates with automated build, test and deployment pipelines
It requires a separate guest OS for each container
It provides tools to create, store, manage and run containers
It is a managed AWS service for running Kubernetes
It is a lightweight container virtualization platform

questions.question: After you create a container image, it can run anywhere that Docker is supported.
questions.explanation: Slide 15 notes: Docker is a portable runtime environment; after you create an image it can go anywhere Docker is supported.

questions.question: Why is instantiating a Docker container fast?
questions.explanation: Slide 16 notes: each container gets a thin read/write layer on top of the image when instantiated; most of the work is read-only because of the file system layers, which makes instantiation fast.
options: Each container boots its own operating system kernel
Each container adds only a thin read/write layer on top of the existing read-only image layers
Containers are stored in the registry already running
Each container copies and rebuilds every image layer at launch

questions.question: Your containerized application must keep customer uploads permanently, even after the container is replaced. Where should this data be stored?
questions.explanation: Slide 16 notes: the read/write layer is not designed for long-term storage; persistent data should be stored in a volume. Treat a container as a compute unit, not a storage unit.
options: In a volume outside the container's read/write layer
In the container's thin read/write layer

questions.question: A container should be thought of as a discrete compute unit, not a storage unit.
questions.explanation: Slide 16 notes: consider a container a discrete compute unit, not a storage unit; persistent data belongs in a volume.

questions.question: You can create only one container from a given container image.
questions.explanation: Slide 16 notes: a container is a runnable instance of an image, and you can create one container or several containers based on that image.

questions.question: You want an image that runs your web application on Ubuntu Linux. According to the course, how is such an image usually built?
questions.explanation: Slide 16 notes and slide 27: images are often based on other images with some customization, for example an Ubuntu image from the registry plus a web server and your application.
options: Take a snapshot of a running VM and upload it to the registry
Base it on an existing Ubuntu image from a registry and customize it with a web server, your app and configuration
Write the entire Ubuntu operating system into the Dockerfile from scratch
Copy the host operating system kernel into the image

questions.question: A container registry can hold only private images; public images cannot be used as a base for other images.
questions.explanation: Slide 16: a container registry holds private or public images that you can base other images on.

questions.question: Each instruction in a Dockerfile creates a writable layer in the image, so the image can be changed after it is built.
questions.explanation: Slides 17 and 20: each instruction creates a read-only layer; because all layers are read-only, the image is an immutable object.

questions.question: Using the course's CentOS web server Dockerfile, match each instruction with what it does (from the Dockerfile comments).
questions.explanation: Slides 19 and 20: FROM sets the base image, RUN updates the OS and installs Apache, EXPOSE opens port 80, ADD copies the shell script, and CMD runs the script when the container is instantiated.

pairs.right: Start with a base image

pairs.left: RUN yum -y update && yum -y install httpd
pairs.right: Update the OS and install Apache
Open the port the web server listens to
Copy the shell script into the image
Run the shell script after the container is instantiated

extra: Push the image to a registry

questions.question: In the simple Dockerfile example, the image starts FROM the latest Ubuntu image and adds CMD echo "Hello World!". What happens?
questions.explanation: Slide 17: you start with the existing Ubuntu image and add a command that echoes Hello World! after the container is instantiated.
options: Hello World! is printed once while the image is being built and never again
The message Hello World! is output after a container is instantiated from the image
A new Ubuntu image is published to Docker Hub

questions.question: Put the steps of the course's Java application Dockerfile in order.
questions.explanation: Slide 18: start with the openjdk 8 image, copy the .jar file into the container, then call Java to run the code; when the container is instantiated, it runs the Java application.
items: Start with the open JDK version 8 image
Copy the .jar file that contains your code from your system to the container
Call Java to run your code when the container is instantiated

questions.question: In a Dockerfile's image layers, which layer is at the bottom of the stack?
questions.explanation: Slide 20 notes: starting from the bottom, the first layer is the base layer (CentOS 7 from FROM), with each later instruction stacked above it; the container's read/write layer sits on top of the image when it runs.
options: The layer created by the last instruction in the file
The base image named in the FROM instruction

questions.question: Why are container images lightweight, small and fast to rebuild compared to other virtualization technologies?
questions.explanation: Slide 20 notes: if you change the Dockerfile and rebuild the image, only the layers that changed are rebuilt, which is part of what makes images lightweight and fast.
options: Images contain no files, only commands
Images are stored compressed inside the container layer
When you change the Dockerfile and rebuild, only the layers that changed are rebuilt
Every rebuild produces a brand new full operating system

questions.question: A monolithic shopping application sees a demand spike only in its cart process. What must happen?
questions.explanation: Slide 35 notes: in a monolith, processes are tightly coupled, so a spike in one process means the entire architecture must be scaled.
options: The cart process is rewritten in a different language
Only the cart service is scaled independently
The entire application architecture must be scaled because the processes are tightly coupled
Nothing, because monolithic processes scale automatically

questions.question: Which of the following describe services in a microservice architecture? Select more than one answer.
questions.explanation: Slide 35 notes: each microservice is an independent component communicating via lightweight APIs, performs a single function, and can be updated, deployed and scaled independently.
options: Services can be updated, deployed and scaled independently
Each service is an independent component that communicates through lightweight API operations
Each service performs a single function that could support multiple applications
All services are tightly coupled and scaled together

questions.question: In a monolithic architecture, a failure in a single process has a smaller impact on availability than in a microservice architecture.
questions.explanation: Slide 35 notes: monoliths add availability risk because many dependent, tightly coupled processes increase the impact of a single process failure.

questions.question: Which development pattern does the course compare the 'designed for failure, disposable' container characteristic to?
questions.explanation: Slide 36: containers start fast, fail fast and release file handlers; the development pattern is like a circuit breaker, with containers added and removed as workloads change.

questions.question: When you run hundreds of hosts and thousands of containers, which challenges must be managed? Select more than one answer.
questions.explanation: Slide 38 lists the challenges of managing containers at scale: state, scheduling of starts and stops, resources on each server, and maximizing availability, resilience and performance.
options: Placing containers to maximize availability, resilience and performance
Writing a separate Dockerfile for every container instance

questions.question: Container orchestration platforms integrate with other services such as networking, persistent storage, security, monitoring and logging.
questions.explanation: Slide 39 notes: orchestration platforms handle scheduling and placement and integrate with services for networking, persistent storage, security, monitoring and logging.

questions.question: Which of the following are true about Amazon ECS? Select more than one answer.
questions.explanation: Slide 40: ECS is a fully managed orchestration service that scales to thousands of containers, schedules placement across managed clusters, and integrates with third-party schedulers and AWS services like IAM, CloudWatch and Route 53.
options: It provides its own schedulers but can also integrate with third-party schedulers
It only stores container images and cannot run them
It scales rapidly to thousands of containers with no additional complexity
It only works with Kubernetes clusters
It integrates with AWS services such as IAM, Amazon CloudWatch and Amazon Route 53

questions.question: A developer pushes images from a laptop and Amazon ECS deploys them to production. How does Amazon ECR protect the images?
questions.explanation: Slide 41 notes: ECR transfers images over HTTPS, automatically encrypts them at rest, and lets you configure per-repository policies restricting access to IAM users, roles or other AWS accounts.
options: It stores images unencrypted but only in a private VPC
It transfers images over HTTPS, automatically encrypts them at rest, and uses repository policies to restrict access to IAM users, roles or other accounts
It encrypts images only when they are deleted
It requires each developer to share a single password

questions.question: Amazon ECR reduces the need to operate your own container repositories or worry about scaling the underlying infrastructure.
questions.explanation: Slide 41 notes: ECR hosts images in a highly available, scalable architecture, so you do not need to operate your own repositories or scale their infrastructure.

questions.question: Before you can push an image to an Amazon ECR repository with Docker, what must you do?
questions.explanation: Slide 44 notes: to push an image into Amazon ECR, you must first authenticate the Docker client to your ECR registry.
options: Authenticate the Docker client to your Amazon ECR registry
Launch an ECS task on Fargate
Convert the Dockerfile to a Kubernetes manifest

questions.question: Put the high-level Amazon ECS workflow in order.
questions.explanation: Slide 42 notes: images are pulled from a registry, you define your application as tasks or services, you choose Fargate or EC2, and ECS then scales and manages your containers for availability.
items: Pull container images from a registry such as Amazon ECR
Define your application as short-running tasks or long-running services
Select a launch type: AWS Fargate or Amazon EC2
Use Amazon ECS to manage, scale and keep containers available

questions.question: Within one application on Amazon ECS, you must choose either Fargate or EC2; the two launch types cannot be mixed.
questions.explanation: Slide 42 notes: you can mix and match the two launch types as needed within your application.

questions.question: With Amazon ECS, container images must come from Amazon ECR; third-party or private registries are not supported.
questions.explanation: Slide 42 notes: the registry can be Amazon ECR, which is one of many AWS services that integrate with ECS, or a third-party or private registry.

questions.question: A team wants to focus on their application and not manage servers, placement, or CPU and memory sizing for their containers. Which ECS launch type fits?
questions.explanation: Slide 43 notes: Fargate is a near-serverless experience where AWS manages the infrastructure, places tasks and ensures each has appropriate CPU and memory.
options: Amazon EC2, because AWS manages the cluster instances for you
AWS Fargate, because AWS manages the infrastructure and task placement
Amazon ECR, because it runs containers serverlessly
Amazon EKS, because it removes the need for worker nodes

questions.question: A company has predictable resource requirements, wants granular control over placement across its own cluster, and wants to use Reserved Instances to reduce cost. Which ECS launch type?
questions.explanation: Slide 43: choose EC2 for more predictable resource requirements or reserved instances; with EC2 you create and manage the cluster and define container placement.

questions.question: Drag each of these workload types to the ECS launch type that suits it.
questions.explanation: Slide 43: Fargate suits large workloads optimized for low overhead; EC2 suits large workloads optimized for price and services with more predictable resource requirements.

items.item: Large workloads optimized for low overhead
Services with more predictable resource requirements

questions.question: Amazon EKS is a proprietary container platform, so applications built for standard Kubernetes must be rewritten before they can run on it.
questions.explanation: Slide 45: EKS is built with the Kubernetes community and is certified conformant and compatible; applications on any standard Kubernetes environment are fully compatible and can be migrated to EKS.

questions.question: A team uses existing Kubernetes tools and plugins on premises. What lets them keep using these tools on Amazon EKS?
questions.explanation: Slide 45 notes: EKS is certified Kubernetes conformant, so you can use existing tools and plugins from partners and the Kubernetes community.
options: Amazon EKS stores the tools in Amazon ECR
Amazon EKS converts Kubernetes apps into ECS tasks
Amazon EKS only supports AWS-built plugins
Amazon EKS is certified Kubernetes conformant

questions.question: Which of the following are true about Amazon EKS? Select more than one answer.
questions.explanation: Slide 45 notes: EKS runs Kubernetes management across multiple AZs to avoid a single point of failure, is secure by default with encrypted channels to worker nodes, and AWS contributes to Kubernetes. Slide 46: worker nodes can be EC2 or Fargate.
options: It runs the Kubernetes management infrastructure across multiple Availability Zones
It can only use Fargate worker nodes
It is secure by default, setting up secure and encrypted channels to worker nodes
AWS contributes to the Kubernetes code base
It is a container image registry

questions.question: Kubernetes is an open-source container management platform that lets you use the same toolset on premises and in the cloud.
questions.explanation: Slide 45 notes: Kubernetes is open source and lets you run any type of containerized application with the same toolset on premises and in the cloud.

questions.question: Put the steps for using Amazon EKS in order.
questions.explanation: Slide 46 notes: you provision an EKS cluster, deploy EC2 or Fargate worker nodes, then connect to EKS and run your Kubernetes applications.
items: Provision an Amazon EKS cluster
Deploy Amazon EC2 or Fargate worker nodes for the cluster
Connect to Amazon EKS
Run your Kubernetes applications
